title: Hooke's law & springs
examples: How do I calculate the spring constant if I know the force and extension?
What is the difference between the elastic limit and the breaking point?
If I connect two springs, which way should I connect them to make them stronger?

explain.say: Today we will learn about how springs behave when we pull them.

items: Force (F): The pulling or pushing force applied.
Extension (x): How much the spring stretches.

explain.say: Hooke's law states that the force is proportional to the extension.
The spring constant, k, tells us how stiff the spring is.
The elastic limit is the maximum stretch before permanent damage occurs.
When connecting springs in series, the total extension adds up.
For springs in parallel, the total force increases while extension stays the same.

faq.q: What does the spring constant k actually measure?
faq.a: It measures the stiffness of the spring. A larger k means the spring is harder to stretch.
asks: What is the unit for k?

faq.q: If I stretch a spring past its elastic limit, what happens?
faq.a: The spring will stay stretched even when I let go, meaning it has permanently deformed.

faq.q: When connecting springs in series, do I add the forces or the extensions?
faq.a: You add the extensions. The total extension is the sum of the individual extensions.
asks: Is it the total stretch that matters?

faq.q: When connecting springs in parallel, do I add the constants or the forces?
faq.a: You add the spring constants, k. This increases the overall stiffness of the setup.
asks: How do I find the total k in parallel?

faq.q: Is Hooke's law always true for springs?
faq.a: No, Hooke's law only applies within the elastic limit of the material.
asks: What are the limits of the law?

facts: Hooke's Law relates force (F) to extension (x) using the spring constant (k).
The equation is written as F equals k times x.
The elastic limit is the point beyond which the spring will not return to its original shape.
In series, the extensions add up, but the force remains the same.

quiz.say: If two identical springs are connected in parallel, what happens to the overall spring constant?
quiz.why: In parallel, the individual spring constants add up, making the combined spring twice as stiff.

wrong.0: This is wrong because multiplication is not the correct method for combining constants in parallel.
wrong.2: This is wrong because connecting them in parallel increases the total resistance to stretching.
wrong.3: This is wrong because adding springs together always increases the overall stiffness.

quiz.say: When connecting springs in series, the total extension is calculated by:
quiz.why: In a series connection, the total stretch is the sum of the stretches of each spring.

wrong.0: This is wrong because division would make the total stretch appear smaller than it really is.
wrong.2: This is wrong because multiplication is not how stretches combine in a line.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the total stretch must account for every spring in the line.
